PACKAGE.JSON EXPORTS DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your package.json "exports" map point at files that actually exist?

Paste your package.json and a listing of the files you actually publish (npm pack --dry-run, git ls-files, or a plain find . -type f) and see every literal target in the exports map — across every subpath, every condition (import/require/types/...), every fallback array — that doesn't exist. That's the difference between a package that works on the maintainer's own machine and one that throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED or Cannot find module the moment a stranger runs npm install.

Nothing is uploaded. Both text boxes are parsed in this browser and never leave your device. This checks existence, not behaviour: it never runs your code, resolves an import graph, or reads a file's contents.

1. Paste your files

2. What's missing

SubpathConditionTargetStatus

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a pre-publish CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — reads only local files, no network call:

node cli.mjs check                          # ./package.json
node cli.mjs check path/to/package.json
node cli.mjs check --json                    # machine-readable

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. Run it after your build step and before npm publish — it checks what's on disk right now, so running it before the build has produced anything will read every export as missing. Exits 1 if any literal export target is missing, so it works as the last gate before a publish that would have broken.

What's checked, and what's deliberately skipped

ShapeHandling
A literal path ("./dist/index.js"), at any subpath, any nesting of conditions, any position in a fallback arrayChecked — reported missing if it doesn't exist
A wildcard target ("./features/*")skipped — resolving one needs matching real files against a pattern, out of scope for v0
A bare specifier ("other-package/subpath")skipped — re-exports another package, nothing on disk to check
null (explicitly blocked subpath)Not a file target, ignored entirely — this is intentional, correct package.json

More: why exports maps drift from what actually publishes, and how to wire this into CI · this checker vs. manually checking each target by eye. Already use publint? See how the two compare.

Common questions

Why does a bad exports target only show up after publish?

On the maintainer's own machine the build has usually already run, so the file the exports map names is sitting right there and everything works. The gap is between what's on disk right now and what actually ends up in the published tarball — a rename during a refactor, a build script that changed its output directory, or an npm publish run before the build step finished, and the first person to find out is a stranger running npm install, not the maintainer.

What is ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED?

Node's own error when code tries to import a subpath that either isn't listed in the package's exports map at all, or is listed but the file it points to isn't there. It replaced Node's older, more forgiving file resolution, so a package.json that shipped exports without checking every target actually exists is exactly the failure mode this tool looks for.

Is this a bundler or a publish tool?

No. It never runs your package, never resolves an import graph, and never reads a file's contents — it only checks whether each literal path the exports map names exists. Wildcard subpaths ("./features/*") and bare-specifier re-exports of another package are listed as not checked, not as passing or failing.

Is my package.json uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the text you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only local files — no network call, ever.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not engineering advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or actually running npm publish --dry-run and testing the tarball yourself. It reports whether a literal path named in "exports" exists on disk against the file list you provided — nothing more, and it is not a guarantee that your package will install or import cleanly. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass on the same repo: .env.example Drift Check and Structured Data Drift Check ask the same "does the doc still match the code" question about a different pair of files, with the same deterministic, no-upload shape. Node Version Drift Check does the same for the Node.js versions declared in engines.node, .nvmrc, the Dockerfile and CI.

Free and open source. If this saved you a broken publish, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-manually-checking-exports-targets.htm.text:
← package.json Exports Drift Check

This checker vs. manually checking each exports target by eye

Names no specific product or company — the comparison is against reading an exports map yourself, a habit every package.json author already has. Manually checking needs no tool: open the exports map, and for each subpath and condition, confirm the file it names actually exists. It works for a map with one or two subpaths. It stops working at the scale a real package's exports field actually reaches, because a present target and a missing one read identically as JSON — nothing about the text says whether the file is there.

What each method is

Manually checking means opening package.json, finding the exports field, and for every subpath and every nested condition (import/require/types/…) confirming the target file is really there — usually by clicking through a file tree or running ls against each path in turn. It costs nothing and needs no tool, and for a small map it is completely reliable: a person who checks two files correctly checks two files correctly, every time.

This tool does the same check mechanically, from two pasted text blocks: a package.json and a listing of the files you actually publish. It flattens every subpath, every nested condition, and every position in a fallback array into one flat list of literal targets, then reports the exact ones missing from the listing — with no install, no publish, and no network call either way.

SubpathConditionTargetOn disk?
.import./esm/index.jsyes
.require./cjs/index.jsyes
.types./types/index.d.tsyes
./buttonimport./esm/button.jsyes
./buttonrequire./cjs/button.jsyes
./buttontypes./types/button.d.tsyes
./modalimport./esm/modal.jsyes
./modalrequire./cjs/modal.jsmissing
./modaltypes./types/modal.d.tsyes
./theme—./cjs/theme.jsyes
./package.json—./package.jsonyes

Eleven literal targets across five subpaths. Ten exist. The one that doesn't — the require condition inside ./modal — is where a maintainer who develops and tests the package entirely through its own ESM import path would never personally exercise the CommonJS fallback, so a rename that left cjs/modal.js behind (or a build step that simply never emitted it) passes every test the maintainer actually ran. Eyeballing the same eleven rows, nothing on the page marks the ninth one as different from the other ten — it is exactly as well-formed a piece of JSON as any target that does exist. Pasted into this tool, the same map and file listing resolve to one finding: 1 export target(s) named in package.json do not exist, naming cjs/modal.js specifically.

QuestionWhere to answer it
My exports map has one or two subpaths and I already know every file it points at. Either — manually checking is completely reliable at this size, and costs nothing.
My exports map nests conditions across a dozen or more subpaths and I want to be sure every literal target still exists. This checker — paste both, get the exact list of missing targets in one click, no signup.
I only test my package through its ESM import path and want to know if a require or types target quietly broke. This checker — it checks every condition the same way, regardless of which one your own tests happen to exercise.
I want to wire this into CI as the last gate before npm publish, reading only local files. Neither needs a tool per se, but only the checker's CLI (cli.mjs) is scriptable and deterministic enough to fail a build on.

This tool needs no account, no install, and no network call: it is a static page that runs entirely in your browser, or a zero-dependency Node CLI that reads only local files.

Common questions

What does eyeballing an exports map get wrong?

Every literal target in an exports map reads the same on the page: a quoted relative path next to a subpath and a condition name. Nothing about the text itself says whether the file at the end of that path actually exists — that's a fact about the filesystem, not about the JSON. A small map (one or two subpaths) is realistic to check by opening each file yourself. A real package's map nests import/require/types conditions and fallback arrays across a dozen or more subpaths, and reading all of them correctly, every time, is exactly the kind of bookkeeping that slips under time pressure — especially for a condition like require that a maintainer who only tests the import path never personally exercises.

Can you give a concrete example?

A package.json declares five subpaths — ".", "./button", "./modal", "./theme", "./package.json" — totalling eleven literal targets once every import/require/types condition is flattened. The files actually published are missing exactly one of them: cjs/modal.js, the require condition inside "./modal". Every other target exists. Pasted into this tool, the package.json and the file listing resolve to one finding: 10 export target(s) exist, 1 export target(s) named in package.json do not exist — and it names cjs/modal.js specifically. Eyeballing the same eleven lines, nothing distinguishes the missing one from the other ten; a maintainer who tests only through the ESM import path (the common case in a codebase and its own tests) would never notice modal's require target was broken until a CommonJS consumer's require() call failed.

Is this tool just automating something obvious?

Reading whether one target file exists is obvious once you already know which line to check. What manual review gets wrong is coverage across the whole map: a deeply nested exports field mixes conditions a maintainer actively exercises (typically the one their own build and tests use) with ones they don't (often require, if the project itself only imports its own code with ESM). This tool doesn't know which condition matters more to any given consumer — it checks every literal target in the map, every subpath, every condition, every fallback-array position, the same way, so coverage doesn't depend on which paths a maintainer happens to run.

Does this replace testing the package after publish?

No. It replaces the step of manually re-reading the exports map to decide whether every target it names is present on disk. A clean result means every literal target you pasted a file listing for exists at that path — it is not a guarantee the package installs or imports cleanly, and it does not resolve wildcard targets or bare-specifier re-exports at all. Verify with npm publish --dry-run and a real install, exactly as this tool's own front page and footer already say.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not engineering advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or actually running npm publish --dry-run and testing the tarball yourself. It reports whether a literal path named in "exports" exists on disk against the file list you provided — nothing more, and it is not a guarantee that your package will install or import cleanly. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

vs-publint.html.text:
← package.json Exports Drift Check

This checker vs. publint

Different scope and a different moment: publint is a broad packaging linter that audits a package you already have installed, packed, or published, against a wide set of publish-readiness rules. This tool does one narrow thing, from two pasted text blocks alone: name every literal exports target that doesn't exist — no install, no publish, no network call.

What each product is for

publint is a free, open-source linter, published as both a website and a npx publint CLI. Its own documentation describes checking a package against a broad set of publish-readiness problems: issues with the exports, main, module, and types fields among them, alongside CJS/ESM resolution mismatches, deprecated fields, and other packaging mistakes that only surface for a consumer after install. The website version points at a package already published to npm (by name and version) or an uploaded tarball; the CLI runs against a local package directory. Today's exact rule list and any change to it are publint's own to state, not repeated here since this session cannot verify them live against publint's own site.

This tool does none of what publint's broader rule set does. It has no install step, reads no node_modules, and never talks to the npm registry. It takes exactly two things you paste — a package.json and a listing of the files you actually publish — and flattens every subpath, every nested condition (import/require/types/...), and every fallback array in the exports map, then reports each literal target that is missing from that listing. A wildcard target or a bare-specifier re-export is reported as not checked, never as passing or failing. Because it needs nothing installed or published, it works on a package.json you are still editing, against a hypothetical file listing of what a build would produce — a question publint's own workflow, built around an already-existing package, is not shaped to answer.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want the broad, well-established publish-readiness audit — CJS/ESM resolution, deprecated fields, and more — against a package that's already installed, packed, or on the registry.publint — that is the audit it is built for.
I want to know right now, for free, exactly which exports targets are missing, from a package.json I'm still editing and a file listing I haven't built yet.This tool — paste both, get the list, nothing installed.
I want a website that checks a package already published to npm by name and version.publint — this tool reads only what you paste, never the registry.
I want a zero-dependency CI gate that runs after my build step and before npm publish, reading only local files with no network call.Either works locally; this tool's CLI (cli.mjs) needs no install of its own.
I want CJS/ESM resolution and other packaging checks beyond whether an exports target file exists.publint — this tool checks existence only, nothing about resolution or module format.
I want the exports map flattened and diffed against a file listing that isn't real yet — planning a refactor, say — with no package to point a tool at.This tool — that's the one job it does, and it needs nothing to exist on disk.

A maintainer can reasonably use both: publint as the broad, periodic publish-readiness audit against a real package, and this tool as a fast, any-time sanity check on the exports map itself — useful even before a build has produced anything to point a broader linter at. This page does not evaluate publint's accuracy or coverage and makes no claim about it either way — it only describes publint's documented product shape and states what this tool does differently. A clean result from either one is not a guarantee your package will install or import cleanly; verify with npm publish --dry-run and a real install.

This tool needs no account, no install, and no network call: it is a static page that runs entirely in your browser, or a zero-dependency Node CLI that reads only local files.

Common questions

Does publint already check exports targets, the way this tool does?

publint's own documentation describes it as a broad packaging linter: it audits a package.json against a wide range of publish-readiness problems — among them, issues with the exports, main, module, and types fields — as one part of a much larger rule set covering CJS/ESM resolution, deprecated fields, and other packaging mistakes. It normally runs against a package you point it at: a name and version already published to npm (via its website), an uploaded tarball, or a local package directory (via its own CLI). This tool does one thing only, from two pasted text blocks with nothing installed or published: flatten every subpath, condition, and fallback array in the exports map and name each literal target that is missing from a file listing you provide.

Should I use this tool or publint?

They overlap on one question and differ on scope and when you can run them. publint is the broader publish-readiness linter — reach for it to catch the wider set of packaging mistakes it documents, against a package that already exists on disk or on the registry. This tool answers one narrower question, before that: given a package.json you are still editing and a hypothetical or planned file listing, which exports targets would be missing right now? That makes it usable earlier — before a build has run, before anything is packed or published — and it needs nothing installed and no network call either way. A maintainer can reasonably use both: this tool as an any-time sanity check on the exports map itself, publint as the broader pre-publish audit.

Is this page affiliated with publint?

No. This page is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by publint or its author. publint is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on publint's own publicly documented product.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not engineering advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or actually running npm publish --dry-run and testing the tarball yourself. It reports whether a literal path named in "exports" exists on disk against the file list you provided — nothing more, and it is not a guarantee that your package will install or import cleanly. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

why-package-json-exports-fields-drift-fr.text:
← Back to package.json Exports Drift Check

Why package.json exports fields drift from what you actually publish

Node's exports field in package.json is a contract: for every subpath it names, there is exactly one file (per condition) that a consumer's import or require resolves to. Unlike Node's older, more forgiving file resolution, a broken entry here doesn't degrade gracefully — it throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED or Cannot find module the instant something tries to use it.

Why it happens: the map is authored once, the build output changes underneath it

A typical library builds ESM and CommonJS output into separate directories, points exports at both, and ships. Then a build tool upgrade renames an output directory, a refactor moves the entry file, or a maintainer runs npm publish straight after a source edit without re-running the build — and nothing forces exports to be re-checked against what the build actually produced. It is the same shape as a changelog that stops matching the commits it describes, or an .env.example that stops matching the code that reads it: one file, hand-authored, drifting from an artifact that changes on its own schedule.

Why this bug is unusually invisible to the maintainer

On the maintainer's own machine, the build has almost always already run by the time they test anything, so the exact file exports names is sitting right there and everything works. The gap is between what's on disk locally right now and what ends up in the tarball a stranger installs — a difference the maintainer has no natural reason to look at, because their own environment never reproduces it. The first person to find out is whoever runs npm install next.

What this tool checks, and what it deliberately doesn't

ShapeHandling
A literal path, any subpath, any condition nesting, any position in a fallback arrayChecked against the file listing / filesystem
A wildcard target (./features/*)Skipped — needs pattern matching against real files, out of scope for v0
A bare specifier re-exporting another packageSkipped — nothing on disk to check
main / module / types top-level fieldsNot read at all in v0 — see the FAQ below

Wiring it into CI as the last gate before publish

Run it as the final step of your publish job, after the build and before npm publish — running it earlier will read every export as missing, because the build hasn't produced anything yet:

- run: npm run build
- run: node ventures/package-exports-drift-check/cli.mjs check
- run: npm publish

The command exits non-zero if any literal export target doesn't exist on disk relative to package.json. For extra confidence against what will actually ship (as opposed to what's on disk), pair it with npm pack --dry-run's file list pasted into the browser tool.

Already run publint as part of your publish checks? See how this tool and publint compare — different scope, and this one needs nothing installed or published.

Common questions

Isn't this what "files" and .npmignore are for?

Those control which files get INTO the tarball. This tool checks a separate question: whether the paths named in "exports" match files that actually exist at all, in the location you're checking (your working tree, or a listing you took from the tarball itself). A file can be correctly included by "files" and still be at the wrong path relative to what "exports" claims — that mismatch is what this catches.

Does npm or Node check this for me at publish time?

No. npm publish packs whatever "files" (or its defaults) selects and uploads it; it does not read "exports" and verify every target resolves to a real file in that tarball. Node only discovers a broken exports target the moment something tries to import it — which, for most maintainers, is the first bug report from a user, not a step in the publish itself.

What about the "main", "module", and "types" fields?

Out of scope for v0, on purpose. "exports" is the field that changed Node's resolution behaviour and is the sharpest, most all-or-nothing failure mode — a wrong entry there can make an entire subpath unimportable rather than just a fallback. "main"/"module"/"types" pointing at missing files is a real but softer version of the same problem, and TypeScript's own tooling (tsc, arethetypeswrong) already checks the "types" case specifically.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report whether a literal path named in a package.json "exports" map exists against a file listing you provided — nothing more. It is not engineering advice, and it is not a guarantee that your package will install or import cleanly. Verify by actually running npm publish --dry-run and testing the tarball before relying on it. Back to the tool.
